issues.legal_issue: Acceptance of rent after a termination notice in a continuing statutory tenancy does not create a new contractual tenancy that erases earlier rent defaults, and repeated defaults exceeding the statutory threshold deprive the tenant of the statutory protection against eviction.
material_facts: The tenancy agreement required monthly rent to be paid by the seventh day of each month, but rent was paid late on eight occasions from September 1954 to April 1955.
After serving a notice terminating the tenancy, the landlord accepted rent, and the tenant maintained that the old tenancy had thereby been revived and continued.
The landlord later served a second termination notice and brought an eviction suit for rent defaults.
The defaults exceeded three occasions within an eighteen-month period.
issues.conclusion: The old tenancy continued with its earlier defaults; the landlord could rely on those defaults, and the tenant was not entitled to the statutory protection against eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 12(1)(i) and 14(3) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, late payment within the meaning of section 12(1)(i) may support recovery of possession, and the tenant loses section 14 protection after more than three such defaults within eighteen months. In a statutory tenancy, acceptance of rent does not assent to a new contractual tenancy but continues the old tenancy: Ganga Dutt Murarka v. Kartik Chandra Das, Anand Nivas (P) Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanjis Pedhi, and Calcutta Credit Corporation Ltd. v. Happy Homes (P) Ltd. The court also referred to section 113 of the Transfer of Property Act on waiver of notice, and relied on the tenant's own position that the old tenancy had continued.

rule.if: eviction_suit_for_rent_default and statutory_tenancy_continued and landlord_accepted_rent_after_termination_notice and tenant_claimed_old_tenancy_continued and defaults_exceeded_protection_threshold

predicates.eviction_suit_for_rent_default: The landlord brought a suit seeking possession on the basis that the tenant had paid rent late.
predicates.statutory_tenancy_continued: The tenant remained in a tenancy protected by rent-control law after a termination notice.
predicates.landlord_accepted_rent_after_termination: The landlord accepted rent after serving a notice terminating the tenancy.
predicates.tenant_claimed_old_tenancy_continued: The tenant maintained that acceptance of rent continued or revived the old tenancy.
predicates.defaults_exceeded_protection_threshold: The tenant's late payments crossed the applicable repeated-default threshold for protection against eviction.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit is based on late rent, the tenancy continues, the landlord accepts rent after a termination notice, the tenant relies on continuation of the old tenancy, and the defaults cross the protection threshold, the tenant is denied protection against eviction for those defaults.

issues.legal_issue: A later rent-control law that changes substantive rights does not apply retrospectively to defaults arising before it commenced when it contains no express or necessarily implied retrospective intent.
material_facts: The landlord accepted rent after defaults before the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 came into force.
The eviction suit was already pending when that Act came into force.
Section 24 of the 1956 Act provided that, when no proceeding for recovery of possession was pending, acceptance of rent for a period of default operated as a waiver of that default.
The court found that section 24 affected the landlord's substantive rights and contained no express or necessarily implied retrospective direction.
issues.conclusion: Section 24 operated prospectively and did not assist the tenant in the pending suit concerning earlier defaults.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 affects substantive rights because it bars a claim based on rent default after the landlord accepts rent for the default period. Under the accepted canon of statutory interpretation, a substantive right is not taken away retrospectively unless the law expressly provides for retrospectivity or clearly implies it. Section 4 preserved pending proceedings under the repealed Act; the court found no language or clear implication making section 24 retrospective.

predicates.rent_eviction_suit_pending_at_new_law_co: A suit seeking possession for rent default was pending when the later law commenced.
predicates.new_waiver_rule_changes_substantive_righ: The later law made acceptance of rent after default operate as a waiver that restricted the landlord's claim based on that default.
predicates.no_express_or_necessary_retroactive_inte: The later law contained neither express language nor a clear implication that its waiver rule applied to earlier events or pending proceedings.

issues.definition: When a rent-default eviction suit is pending at the commencement of a later law, that law changes substantive rights, and it shows no express or necessarily implied intent to apply retrospectively, its waiver rule applies prospectively only.
